title: Sixth commandment (CCC 2337–2347)
hook: chastity as integration, the person whole and at peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth commandment and the body: health as a gift, the dead treated with respect. Your line was care, not worship. What kindness did you do for your body? Day one thousand one hundred thirty.

A guitar sits on a stand by the window. Five strings are in tune. One has slipped, just slightly. Play any chord, and the whole thing sounds a little wrong, though it's hard to say why. Tighten that one string, and suddenly every chord rings. Nothing was added. Something was brought into agreement with the rest. Hold on to that picture. Today's word can sound like only a no. The Catechism describes it as a kind of tuning.
screen: `FIVE STRINGS IN TUNE.` → `ONE HAS SLIPPED.` → `EVERY CHORD RINGS.`

segments.voice: The commandment in the Douay-Rheims is brief: "Thou shalt not commit adultery." The Catechism reads it widely, and it opens with a word that might surprise: chastity. And it defines chastity as integration. Chastity, it says, means the successful integration of sexuality within the person, and so the inner unity of a human being in body and spirit. The person, whole. Sexuality, in this teaching, isn't the enemy. It becomes personal and truly human, the Catechism says, when it's woven into the relationship of one person to another, in the complete and lifelong gift of a man and a woman to each other. Then it adds a line: chastity tolerates neither a double life nor duplicity in speech. The person who lives one way in public and another in private isn't whole. Next, the Catechism calls chastity an apprenticeship in self-mastery, a training in human freedom. Either we govern our passions and find peace, it says, or we let ourselves be ruled by them. And it's honest that this is long work. Self-mastery, it says, is never acquired once and for all. It takes effort at every stage of life, with growth that has its own stages, its own setbacks. It's a virtue, but also a gift, a grace, from the Holy Spirit. The last note is the warmest. Chastity, the Catechism says, blossoms in friendship. A person at peace inside can be a true friend, giving themselves without grabbing. And elsewhere it adds that every baptized person is called to chastity, each according to their state of life: married, single, or consecrated. Like the string on the guitar: not removed, brought into tune.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT COMMIT ADULTERY.` · `CHASTITY: THE PERSON, WHOLE.` · `NO DOUBLE LIFE.` · `IT BLOSSOMS IN FRIENDSHIP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat others as whole persons. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people you'll see today: at work, on the street, on a screen. Notice how easily a person can shrink to one thing: a body, a job title, a use, an obstacle. Choose one person and let them grow back to full size in your mind: someone's child, with a history, hopes, a tired day. If you pray, you can ask for the grace to see people whole. If you don't, just hold that one person, whole, for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Chastity. The integration of sexuality within the person: body and spirit at one, no double life, a self-mastery that frees a person for friendship and gift. Today's word.
Your line: whole, not divided. Today, notice one place where your words and your life could match a little better, and close the gap by one step. Day one thousand one hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Catholics are taught that chastity is for everyone, lived differently by the married, the single and the consecrated; it's supported by prayer, confession, friendship and modesty.

original.note: Latin: purity, chastity; the Church's word for this virtue.

trapdoor: what you thought: chastity means just saying no.
what it means: the integration of sexuality within the person, so body and spirit are one and the person is free to love.
what a scholar hears: an apprenticeship in self-mastery, 'the school of the gift of the person', blossoming in friendship.
